title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to evaluate whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, artifact‑grounded interpretation, and recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configuration is central to network operations (NetOps). Large language models (LLMs) can rapidly synthesize configuration artifacts from high‑level intent, but probabilistic generation risks omission, misordering, and unsafe commands. Prior work therefore advocates hybrid generate→verify→repair architectures—pairing probabilistic generators with deterministic validators/simulators and bounded repair loops—to reduce operational risk. However, rigorous preregistered evaluations that quantify how tightly bounded guarded pipelines change first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics remain limited. We ask: Can a minimal guarded pipeline (single‑shot LLM generation + frozen deterministic validator + ≤1 automated repair iteration) reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation on a deterministically seeded paired intent→configuration task set? Our contributions: (1) a preregistered paired experiment (cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) with deterministic task seeds and archived per‑task artifacts; (2) confirmatory statistics computed from the archived artifacts; (3) an artifact‑grounded post‑hoc sensitivity bound tied to observed discordance; (4) practical, artifact‑traceable design recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory studies.
sections.related_work: Recent system demonstrations show LLMs can synthesize intent→configuration artifacts in lab settings but document failure modes (misordering, omission, overconfidence) that threaten safety [10.1002/nem.2313]. Verifier‑assisted and retrieval‑augmented pipelines in adjacent domains (medical QA, code repair) reduce factual errors and motivate guarded NetOps architectures [10.36227/techrxiv.176784505.56675782/v1, 10.2139/ssrn.6608518]. Classical deterministic network verification (e.g., header‑space and specification checking) provides algorithmic foundations for validators that can statically check reachability and policy constraints without live execution [10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Surveys and architectures emphasize generate→verify→repair and the need for provenance/auditability and human‑oversight in production NetOps [10.6028/nist.ai.100-2e2023]. Our study executes a preregistered paired evaluation that measures first‑pass validity under an explicit frozen validator+bounded repair floor‑guardrail, connecting these literatures with confirmatory evidence.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: The study was preregistered (cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) before observing outcomes. Confirmatory hypotheses: H1 — guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) vs single‑shot generation; H2 — ≤1 repair iteration recovers ≥75% of initially invalid outputs. The preregistration documented a planning assumption baseline pass rate = 0.40 used for power planning; we report it here because it materially affects interpretation.

Design and sampling: Paired within‑task design with 300 deterministically generated seeds (fixed task generator). For each seed a single shared LLM candidate was produced (shared_initial_candidate) and served as the baseline response; the guarded arm then validated that same candidate and invoked at most one automated repair if violations were reported. Planned episodes = 600 (two episodes per seed), initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. Shared‑candidate pairing isolates the incremental effect of validator+repair on a single proposed plan at the cost of higher within‑pair correlation (fewer informative discordant pairs).

Model and provider settings: The declared generation model in the execution contract was gpt-5-mini. The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 301. The archived execution/model_configuration.json records model fields requested for the run (path: execution/model_configuration.json). That artifact records the model parameter "temperature": null. A null/unset temperature in the recorded configuration is not evidence that sampling was deterministic (temperature=0); sampling determinism therefore was unspecified in the archived configuration and generator variance could be affected by nonfixed sampling settings. This unspecified sampling determinism is a documented inferential limitation of the run and is treated in the analysis and sensitivity plans.

Validator and repair semantics: The frozen deterministic validator canonicalized outputs to a normalized AST and applied static checks derived from explicit workflow and dependency policies encoded in the task payloads (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints). Scoring rule: full intent‑constraint validation—success only when normalized_configuration satisfies required_sequence and expected_final_state constraints and all workflow policies. The preregistered repair adapter received the shared candidate plus structured violation codes and was restricted to a single automated repair attempt per episode; post‑repair outputs were revalidated by the same deterministic validator.

Contamination, exclusions, and analysis: Preregistered deterministic contamination checks used normalized‑AST equality and near‑duplicate lexical thresholds; exact duplicates would trigger deterministic exclusion/replacement from a reserve set. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05); paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for absolute paired difference (10,000 resamples, explicit seed). Missingness policy: drop pairs only if both calls failed ('complete_pair_primary'); sensitivity analyses treat failed calls as failures. All seeds, per‑task artifacts, validator traces, repair prompts/responses, and analysis code were archived in the execution manifest.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (artifact‑derived): planned episodes = 600; completed = 600; complete pairs analyzed = 300; model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial + 1 repair). No provider or infrastructure failures occurred; no deterministic contamination exclusions were required. Primary outcomes (archived counts): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency (guarded vs baseline): n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0 (archive: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv).

Inferential results (preregistered): exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00 on the observed contingency. Observed absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Repair outcomes (H2): the single automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1); Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0].

Post‑hoc sensitivity bound (artifact‑grounded): The observed discordant pair count is 1, which imposes a hard limit on resolvable absolute paired difference = 1/300 ≈ 0.00333. The preregistered target (≥50% relative reduction from planned baseline 0.40 → absolute ≈ +0.30) would have required ~90 net discordant pairs favoring guarded outputs; the observed near‑ceiling baseline removed the statistical headroom to detect the preregistered effect. Detailed per‑task validator traces showing the single corrected failure and its repair are archived in the execution bundle.
sections.discussion: The archived contingency (n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0) directly constrains inference: with only one discordant pair the exact McNemar test and bootstrap CI necessarily reflect extremely small resolvable absolute improvements (here ≈0.00333). The preregistered power plan assumed baseline = 0.40; the observed baseline ≈0.997 collapses that plan. Practical lessons (artifact‑traceable): (1) when planning remediation experiments, calibrate task difficulty or adversarially augment tasks to produce a nontrivial baseline failure prevalence or target discordant count aligned with the planned absolute/relative effect; (2) explicitly preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets and incorporate their effects into power calculations (shared‑candidate pairing increases within‑pair correlation, reducing expected discordance); (3) if runtime semantics matter, integrate emulation/simulation stages and preregister how emulator outcomes map to success/failure. The frozen deterministic validator produced structured traces (normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes) that are essential for actionable failure diagnosis and reproducible post‑mortems. The run demonstrates that a validator+bounded repair can correct at least some invalid candidates without human intervention, but the operational value depends on baseline error prevalence and validator coverage. All diagnostic claims above are supported by archived artifacts in the execution manifest.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) comparing single‑shot LLM generation (gpt-5-mini) to a guarded pipeline with a frozen deterministic validator and a single automated repair attempt. Observed outcomes: baseline 299/300 valid; guarded 300/300 valid; single automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output. The observed near‑ceiling baseline contradicted the preregistered planning assumption (baseline = 0.40), removing statistical headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction. Future confirmatory NetOps evaluations should (a) calibrate task difficulty or adversarially augment tasks to ensure sufficient initial failures or discordant pairs for the planned estimand, (b) preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets explicitly, and (c) include emulation when runtime effects are relevant. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, the execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement to permit reproduction of reported counts and intervals.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.
The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicts that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
